paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Do you read while listening to music? Do you watch television while finishing your homework? People with these habits are called multitaskers. Multitaskers appear to complete two tasks at once by dividing their attention. Thomas Lehman, a psychology researcher, argues that people never truly do several things simultaneously. Someone may read while listening to music, but the brain can focus on only one task at a time: reading a book causes the listener to ignore some of the song’s words. When people think they are completing two tasks efficiently, they are really dividing their attention. Listening to music also makes people less aware of their surroundings. We have all spoken to friends who do not respond properly, perhaps because they are listening to someone else or reading a text on a smartphone and do not hear us. Lehman calls this phenomenon ‘email voice’.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Computers and their spin-offs, such as smartphones and mobile phones, have changed the world. Now that most people own a personal device, such as a smartphone or laptop, they frequently read, watch or listen to virtual information. This increases the prevalence of multitasking in everyday life. At work, people use a computer and mobile phone while colleagues may stop by at any time to speak to them. In professional meetings, where participants would normally focus on and listen to one another, people are increasingly likely to keep a mobile phone in their lap and communicate silently with others. Even inventions such as the cordless phone have increased multitasking. In the past, when a wall-mounted telephone rang, a housewife had to stop what she was doing to answer it. She would sit down and chat without doing the laundry, sweeping or answering the door. Modern technology, by contrast, allows us to continue our daily tasks while communicating.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Earl Miller, an expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studied the prefrontal cortex, which controls the brain while a person multitasks. The size of this cortex varies between species: it constitutes about one-third of the human brain, compared with only 4–5 per cent in dogs and around 15 per cent in monkeys. Its greater size in humans may enable more flexible and accurate multitasking. Miller wanted to determine whether the cortex truly processed information from two tasks simultaneously. He presented participants with visual stimuli in a way that mimicked multitasking, then attached sensors to their heads to record the brain’s electrical patterns. These sensors showed whether neurons were actually processing two different tasks. Miller found that neurons became active in only one area at a time, never simultaneously.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: David Meyer, a professor at the University of Michigan, studied young adults in a similar experiment. He instructed them to solve mathematics problems while classifying simple words into categories. Meyer found that when people think they are doing several jobs at once, they are actually switching between them. Although the participants attempted both tasks simultaneously and eventually completed both, the work took longer overall than it would have if they had focused on one task at a time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: People sacrifice efficiency when they multitask. Gloria Mark used office workers as her research subjects and found that they were constantly multitasking. On average, workers were interrupted about every 11 minutes. Doing different jobs at once may save time, but being faster does not necessarily make people more efficient. People are as likely to interrupt themselves as they are to be interrupted by outside sources. Mark found that, in an office, an employee would stop about every 12 minutes for no apparent reason to check a website, call someone or write an email. If employees concentrated for more than 20 minutes, they felt distressed. She suggested that the average person may have a short attention span. This may be natural, but others argue that new technology is responsible. With mobile phones and computers always at hand, people never run out of distractions. Media formats—including advertisements, music, news articles and television programmes—are also becoming shorter, so people are accustomed to attending to information only briefly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Although focusing on a single task is the most efficient way for the brain to work, this approach is not always practical. People naturally feel more comfortable and efficient in environments that offer a variety of tasks. Edward Hallowell says that multitasking, external interruptions and self-distraction cause substantial losses of workplace efficiency. Fortunately, improvements need not involve dramatic changes. No one is suggesting banning email or making employees perform only one task. However, common activities such as group meetings would be more efficient if mobile phones, a frequent distraction, were prohibited. Individuals can apply similar methods to prevent self-distraction. Instead of arriving at the office and immediately checking every email for new tasks, they could dedicate the first hour of the day to one job. Timing oneself is a useful way to reduce distraction and complete tasks efficiently one by one, instead of slowing down through multitasking.
